entries.title: Place value and changing bases
headings: The idea: a digit counts bundles
Reading a numeral: base b to decimal
Worked examples: base b to decimal
Writing a number in base b: repeated division
Worked examples: decimal to base b
How many digits does a number need?
When the base is the unknown
entries.text: Every number a digital system stores is a row of digits, and every digit means how many of something. In this lesson you learn to read a numeral in any base, to write any number in any base, to move between bases, to count how many digits a number needs, and to solve the GATE puzzles where the base itself is the unknown. By the end, a question like "for which base b is (312)_b \div (20)_b = (13.1)_b?" will be a two-minute calculation, not a guess. Where this fits This is the first lesson of Digital Logic, and almost everything later leans on it. Binary, octal and hexadecimal (next lesson) are just bases 2, 8 and 16. Fractions and fixed point (Lesson 3) extend place value to the right of the point. Signed numbers (Lesson 4) reuse the same digits with one place given a negative weight. Later chapters read counter states, memory addresses and IEEE-754 fields with exactly the tools built here. The idea: a digit counts bundles Think of a shop that only uses bundles of three: loose items, packets of 3, boxes of 3 packets (9 items), crates of 3 boxes (27 items). To record 46 items you fill crates first: one crate (27), then two boxes (18), no packets, and one loose item. The record reads 1 2 0 1. Each position holds the number of bundles of one size, and the sizes grow by the same factor (here 3) as you move left. A position can never hold 3 or more, because three of anything would be packed into one bundle of the next size. That one rule, "pack as soon as you reach the base", is all of positional notation. Our everyday decimal is the same shop with bundles of ten. An odometer is the same shop in motion. Watch a counter whose wheels only know the digits 0, 1 and 2: when a wheel would reach 3 it rolls back to 0 and nudges its neighbour forward. Notice what the counter shows after three counts: 10. In base 3, "10" means one bundle of three and nothing loose, which is three. That is why "10" means the base itself in every base: ten in decimal, two in binary, sixteen in hexadecimal. Fix a whole number b \ge 2, the base (also called the radix). A base-b numeral is a string of digits d_k d_{k-1} \dots d_1 d_0, optionally followed by a radix point and more digits d_{-1} d_{-2} \dots, where every digit satisfies 0 \le d_i \le b-1. Its value is (d_k \dots d_1 d_0 . d_{-1} d_{-2} \dots)_b \;=\; \sum_i d_i \, b^{\,i}. d_i is the digit in position i, counted from 0 just left of the point. b^{\,i} is the place value (weight) of position i: \dots, b^2, b, 1, b^{-1}, b^{-2}, \dots Digits ten to thirty-five are written A to Z, so in hexadecimal A = 10, B = 11, …, F = 15. The subscript names the base: (1201)_3, (2D)_{16}. A numeral with no subscript is decimal. Here is that definition doing its work: the same four digits, first read in base 3 and then in base 5. Only the place values change. In base b the only digits are 0, 1, \dots, b-1. A numeral that contains a digit d is a valid base-b numeral only when b > d, so the base is at least one more than the largest digit. For example (4072)_b forces b \ge 8, and (19)_8 is not an octal numeral at all. Why insist on this? Two reasons, and both matter for GATE. First, a digit equal to b or more would be a full bundle that should have been carried into the next place, so allowing it would let one number have several spellings ((13)_2 would equal (101)_2). Second, in every "find the base" question the digit limit is the condition that throws away fake solutions. The equation alone is never the whole question. Which of these are valid numerals? (3021)_3, (777)_8, (1G)_{16}, (10)_2. (777)_8 and (10)_2 are valid. (3021)_3 uses the digit 3, which needs base 4 or more. (1G)_{16} uses G = 16, which needs base 17 or more. A digit says how many bundles; its position says which bundle size, b^{\,i}. Every digit is at most b-1, so the base exceeds the largest digit. "10" in base b is b itself. Reading a numeral: base b to decimal To find the value of a numeral, you simply add up digit × place value. There are two ways to organise that sum, and you should be fluent in both. Expansion. By the definition, a numeral with digits d_k \dots d_0 is worth N = d_k b^k + d_{k-1} b^{k-1} + \dots + d_1 b + d_0 . Horner's form. Every term except the last has a factor b, so take it out. Inside the bracket every term except the last again has a factor b; take it out again, and repeat: \begin{aligned} N &= \big(d_k b^{k-1} + d_{k-1} b^{k-2} + \dots + d_1\big)\, b + d_0 \\ &= \Big(\big(d_k b^{k-2} + \dots + d_2\big)\, b + d_1\Big)\, b + d_0 \\ &= \Big(\dots\big((d_k\, b + d_{k-1})\, b + d_{k-2}\big)\, b + \dots\Big)\, b + d_0 . \end{aligned} So you can read a numeral left to right with a single running total t: start with t = 0 and, for each digit d, replace t by t \cdot b + d. After the last digit, t = N. Sanity check. For (1201)_3 the expansion gives 27 + 18 + 0 + 1 = 46, and the chain gives 0 \to 1 \to 1\cdot 3 + 2 = 5 \to 5 \cdot 3 + 0 = 15 \to 15 \cdot 3 + 1 = 46. The two forms agree, as they must, because they are the same sum with the brackets moved. Fraction digits. A digit d_{-j} after the point is worth d_{-j}\, b^{-j}, so (0.8)_{16} = 8/16 = 0.5 and (0.101)_2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac18 = 0.625. Keep one running total. For each digit, multiply the total by the base and add the digit. For (11010)_2: 1 \to 3 \to 6 \to 13 \to 26. Why it works: it is the bracketed form from the derivation, evaluated from the inside out. When it fails: never for whole numbers. For fraction digits it does not apply directly; read those by place value (or run Horner on the digits and divide by b^{\,f}, where f is the number of fraction digits). Worked examples: base b to decimal Find the decimal value of (11010)_2. Write the place values under the digits, starting with 2^0 = 1 on the right. \begin{array}{ccccc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 16 & 8 & 4 & 2 & 1 \end{array} Add the place values that sit under a 1: 16 + 8 + 2 = 26. Check with Horner: 1 \to 2\cdot1+1 = 3 \to 2\cdot3+0 = 6 \to 2\cdot6+1 = 13 \to 2\cdot13+0 = 26.

entries.title: Binary, octal and hex: grouping and arithmetic
headings: Between octal, hex and base 4: always through binary
Worked examples: octal, hex and base 4
Sums of powers of 16, and counting 1s
Worked examples: arithmetic in base 8 and 16
entries.text: Binary is the language of the hardware, but long strings of bits are hard for people to read. Octal and hexadecimal fix that, and they fix it for free: because 8 and 16 are powers of 2, you convert by cutting the bit string into groups, with no division at all. In this lesson you learn why grouping works, how to do it without the classic off-by-a-group slip, how to move between octal, hex and base 4 through binary, how to read a "powers of 16" sum straight off as hex, and how to add, subtract and multiply directly in base 8 or 16. Where this fits Lesson 1 gave the general tools: expand to read, divide to write. They work for every base, but for bases 2, 4, 8 and 16 they are the slow road. Everything in later chapters is written in these bases: memory addresses and instruction fields in hex, Unix permissions in octal, K-map cells and register contents in binary. The 2's-complement patterns of Lesson 4 are also usually given in hex. Why grouping works In base 2 the place values are 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, … Look at them three at a time from the right: (1, 2, 4), then (8, 16, 32) which is 8 × (1, 2, 4), then (64, 128, 256), which is 64 × (1, 2, 4). Each block of three places is the first block scaled by a power of 8. So a block of three bits is a number from 0 to 7 counting units of 8^0, the next block counts units of 8^1, the next units of 8^2. That is exactly an octal digit per block. It is like paying with ₹10 notes bundled in hundreds: a bundle is an exact multiple of a note, so you can count bundles without unpacking them. Blocks of four places scale by 16 the same way, which gives hexadecimal. Let k \ge 1. To convert between base 2 and base 2^k, split the bits into groups of k starting at the radix point and moving outward (leftward for the integer part, rightward for the fraction), pad the outermost groups with zeros to a full k bits, and replace each group by the base-2^k digit with the same value. Read backwards, each base-2^k digit becomes exactly k bits. k = 2: base 4 (2 bits per digit) k = 3: octal (3 bits per digit) k = 4: hexadecimal (4 bits per digit) Idea first: collect the binary expansion in blocks of k terms; each block is a multiple of a power of 2^k. Write an integer as N = \sum_{i} b_i 2^i and gather the terms by i = kj + t with 0 \le t \le k - 1: N = \sum_{j} \Big( \sum_{t=0}^{k-1} b_{kj+t}\, 2^{t} \Big)\, 2^{kj} = \sum_j c_j\, (2^k)^{j}, \qquad c_j = \sum_{t=0}^{k-1} b_{kj+t}\, 2^t . Each c_j is the value of the j-th block of k bits, so 0 \le c_j \le 2^k - 1: a legal base-2^k digit. By the uniqueness of base-2^k numerals (Lesson 1), the c_j are the base-2^k digits of N. Fractions work the same way with negative j: the block nearest the point holds b_{-1}, \dots, b_{-k}. The blocks must be aligned on the point because that is where j = 0 starts. A zero added to the left of the integer part has place value 2^i times 0, and a zero added to the right of the fraction has place value 2^{-i} times 0, so neither changes the number: (101)_2 = (0101)_2 and (0.11)_2 = (0.110)_2. A zero inserted anywhere else pushes the bits after it to new places. For example, padding the fraction .11 on the left to .011 moves both 1s one place right and halves the value: (0.11)_2 = 0.75 but (0.011)_2 = 0.375. Sanity check. (0.11)_2 = 0.75 = 6/8 = (0.6)_8, which is what grouping .110 gives. Memorise the sixteen hex digits as bits, with their count of 1s. An octal digit is just the last three bits of the same row (0 to 7 only). Write (110101)_2 in octal and in hex. Threes from the right: 110\;101 → (65)_8. Fours from the right: 11\;0101 → pad to 0011\;0101 → (35)_{16}. Both equal 53. Because 8 = 2^3 and 16 = 2^4, one octal digit is exactly 3 bits and one hex digit is exactly 4 bits. Group from the point outward; pad only at the outer ends. Worked examples: grouping whole numbers Write (1011010)_2 in octal. Cut threes from the right: 1\;011\;010. Pad the leftmost group: 001\;011\;010. 001 = 1, 011 = 3, 010 = 2, so the numeral is (132)_8. Check: (1011010)_2 = 64 + 16 + 8 + 2 = 90 and (132)_8 = 64 + 24 + 2 = 90. (1011010)_2 = (132)_8 Write (101110111)_2 in hexadecimal. 1\;0111\;0111. 0001\;0111\;0111. 0001 = 1, 0111 = 7, 0111 = 7: (177)_{16}. (101110111)_2 = 256 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 375, and (177)_{16} = 256 + 112 + 7 = 375. (101110111)_2 = (177)_{16} Write (546)_8 in hexadecimal. 5 \to 101, 4 \to 100, 6 \to 110: the bits are 101\,100\,110. 1\;0110\;0110, padded to 0001\;0110\;0110. 1, 6, 6: (166)_{16}. (546)_8 = 320 + 32 + 6 = 358 and (166)_{16} = 256 + 96 + 6 = 358. (546)_8 = (166)_{16} Write (3F2C)_{16} in octal. 3\;F\;2\;C \to 0011\;1111\;0010\;1100. 0\;011\;111\;100\;101\;100. Read the groups: 0, 3, 7, 4, 5, 4, so the numeral is (37454)_8. (3F2C)_{16} = 3\cdot4096 + 15\cdot256 + 2\cdot16 + 12 = 16172, and (37454)_8 = 3\cdot4096 + 7\cdot512 + 4\cdot64 + 5\cdot8 + 4 = 16172. (3F2C)_{16} = (37454)_8 A student writes (1010110)_2 in hex by cutting fours from the left: 1010\;110. What goes wrong? From the left: 1010 = A and 110 is padded to 0110 = 6, giving (A6)_{16} = 166. From the right: 101\;0110, padded to 0101\;0110, gives (56)_{16}. (1010110)_2 = 64 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 86 = (56)_{16}. The wrong grouping is almost double. (56)_{16}. Grouping from the left gives (A6)_{16}, a classic distractor. Groups start at the radix point. For a whole number that is the right end. Cutting from the left shifts every group and gives a wrong numeral that often appears as an option: for (657)_8 = (110\,101\,111)_2 the correct hex is 1AF, but cutting fours from the left gives 1101\;0111\;1 \to D7 followed by a padded 1000 = 8, i.e. D78. Worked examples: grouping fractions Write (0.1011)_2 in hexadecimal. The first four bits after the point: 1011. 1011 = B, so (0.1011)_2 = (0.B)_{16}. \tfrac12 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac1{16} = \tfrac{11}{16} and (0.B)_{16} = \tfrac{11}{16}. entries.title: Fractions and fixed-point numbers
headings: The idea: cutting a cake in halves
Converting a fraction into base b
Worked examples: fractions to binary and other bases
entries.text: Not every number is whole. A sensor reading, a filter coefficient or a price needs digits after the point, and the hardware has to store them in a fixed number of bits. In this lesson you learn to convert a fraction into any base by repeated multiplication, to predict before you start whether the digits will stop or repeat for ever, to bound the error when you cut them off, and to read and design fixed-point formats: how far they reach, how finely they step, and exactly which values they can hold. GATE asks all four of these. Where this fits Lesson 1 showed that the digits after the point are worth b^{-1}, b^{-2}, \dots, and Lesson 2 grouped fraction bits rightward from the point. Here we go the other way, from a decimal fraction to its digits. Fixed point is the simplest way real numbers live in hardware; Chapter 8 replaces it with floating point, where the point moves. The question "is this value exactly representable?" comes back there in the same form. The idea: cutting a cake in halves You may cut a cake only in half, then cut pieces in half again, and so on. You can serve exactly a half, a quarter, three-eighths, five-sixteenths: any sum of these binary pieces. But you can never serve exactly one fifth of the cake, however many times you cut: you can only get closer and closer (a quarter is too much, three-sixteenths too little, …). That is binary fractions in a nutshell. The pieces available are \tfrac12, \tfrac14, \tfrac18, \dots, and a value is exactly representable only if it is a finite sum of them. A base-10 "cake" can be cut into tenths, so it serves one fifth (0.2) easily, but it cannot serve one third. Which fractions come out exactly depends on the base. Converting a fraction into base b Let x = (0.d_1 d_2 d_3 \dots)_b, a fraction with 0 \le x < 1. Multiply by b: every digit moves one place left, so b \cdot x = (d_1 . d_2 d_3 \dots)_b = d_1 + (0.d_2 d_3 \dots)_b . The integer part of b\,x is the first digit d_1, and the fraction part is a new fraction whose first digit is d_2. Repeat on the fraction part. Rule: multiply the fraction by b, peel off the integer part as the next digit, keep the fraction part, repeat. The digits come out first to last, so read them top to bottom (the opposite of repeated division). Stop when the fraction part is 0, or when it repeats. Sanity check. 0.625 \times 2 = 1.25 (digit 1), 0.25 \times 2 = 0.5 (digit 0), 0.5 \times 2 = 1.0 (digit 1), fraction 0: (0.101)_2 = \tfrac12 + \tfrac18 = 0.625. ✓ Mixed numbers: convert the integer part by repeated division and the fraction part by repeated multiplication, then join them at the point. When the fraction part comes back to a value it had before, the same rows repeat for ever and so do the digits. That is a recurring expansion. Watch it happen for 0.1: Repeated division (integers) is read from the bottom up; repeated multiplication (fractions) is read from the top down. Mixing them up reverses the fraction digits: 0.625 would come out as 0.101 either way, but 0.8125 = (0.1101)_2 would be misread as (0.1011)_2 = 0.6875. Worked examples: fractions to binary and other bases Write 0.40625 in binary. 0.40625 \times 2 = 0.8125 → bit 0. Keep 0.8125. 0.8125 \times 2 = 1.625 → bit 1, keep 0.625. Then 0.625 \times 2 = 1.25 → bit 1, keep 0.25. 0.25 \times 2 = 0.5 → bit 0. 0.5 \times 2 = 1.0 → bit 1, fraction 0: stop. (0.01101)_2 = \tfrac14 + \tfrac18 + \tfrac1{32} = \tfrac{13}{32} = 0.40625. 0.40625 = (0.01101)_2 Write 13.375 in binary. Integer: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = (1101)_2 (by repeated division or by powers of 2). 0.375 \times 2 = 0.75 → 0; 0.75 \times 2 = 1.5 → 1; 0.5 \times 2 = 1.0 → 1, stop. So 0.375 = (0.011)_2. 13.375 = (1101.011)_2. (1101.011)_2 Write 0.3 in binary, keep six bits, and bound the error. 0.3 \to 0.6 (0), 0.6 \to 1.2 (1), 0.2 \to 0.4 (0), 0.4 \to 0.8 (0), 0.8 \to 1.6 (1), 0.6 \to 1.2 (1), … 0.3 = (0.0\overline{1001})_2 = 0.0\,1001\,1001\,1001\dots Six bits: (0.010011)_2 = \tfrac{19}{64} = 0.296875. The error is 0.3 - 0.296875 = 0.003125 < 2^{-6} = 0.015625. 0.3 = (0.0\overline{1001})_2 \approx (0.010011)_2, with truncation error 0.003125. Write 45.8125 in hexadecimal. 45 = 16 \cdot 2 + 13, 2 = 16\cdot 0 + 2: (2D)_{16}. 0.8125 \times 16 = 13.0 → digit D, fraction 0: stop. (2D.D)_{16} = 45 + \tfrac{13}{16} = 45.8125. 45.8125 = (2D.D)_{16} Write 0.7 in octal. 0.7 \to 5.6 (5), 0.6 \to 4.8 (4), 0.8 \to 6.4 (6), 0.4 \to 3.2 (3), 0.2 \to 1.6 (1), 0.6 \to 4.8 (4), … 0.7 = (0.5\overline{4631})_8: one non-repeating digit, then a period of four. (0.5\overline{4631})_8. A recurring expansion may start after some non-repeating digits. Fraction → base b: multiply by b, peel the integer part, keep the fraction, read top to bottom. It stops when the fraction becomes 0 and recurs when a fraction part repeats. Which fractions stop? Write a rational number in lowest terms as p/q. Its base-b expansion terminates if and only if every prime factor of q divides b. Otherwise it is recurring. Base 2: p/q terminates exactly when q is a power of 2. So 0.25 = 1/4 and 0.375 = 3/8 are exact; 0.1 = 1/10, 0.2 = 1/5 and 1/3 recur. Base 10: q may have only the primes 2 and 5. So 1/8 = 0.125 terminates but 1/3 does not. Idea first: a terminating base-b fraction is an integer divided by a power of b, so it can only have denominators built from the primes of b. (\Rightarrow) If x = (0.d_1 \dots d_k)_b, then x = m / b^k with m = (d_1 \dots d_k)_b an integer. So p/q = m/b^k, i.e. p\, b^k = m\, q. Since \gcd(p, q) = 1, q divides b^k, so every prime factor of q is a prime factor of b. (\Leftarrow) If every prime of q divides b, choose k at least as large as every exponent in q's factorisation. Then q divides b^k, say b^k = q\,s, and p/q = p\,s / b^k, which is an integer divided by b^k: a numeral with at most k digits after the point. To ask "is this decimal exact in binary?", write it as a fraction in lowest terms and look at the denominator. 0.375 = 3/8: power of 2, exact. 0.05 = 1/20: has a 5, recurs. entries.title: Place value and changing bases
headings: Reading a number in any base
Why every number has one spelling
entries.text: A digit's value depends on where it sits. That one idea, place value, is all you need to read a number written in any base. The big idea Pay ₹347 with notes and coins: 3 hundred-rupee notes, 4 tens, 7 ones. The digit says how many; the position says of what size. Base 2 works the same way, only the bundles are 1, 2, 4, 8, … instead of 1, 10, 100. In base b, the digit in position i (counting from 0 on the right) is worth d_i \cdot b^{\,i}. Every digit must satisfy 0 \le d_i < b. Radix is another word for base. GATE papers use both. Reading a number in any base Add up digit × place value over every position: N = d_k b^k + \dots + d_1 b + d_0 = \sum_{i=0}^{k} d_i\, b^{\,i} Factor out b again and again and the same sum becomes a chain of "multiply, then add": N = \big( \dots ( d_k\, b + d_{k-1} )\, b + \dots \big)\, b + d_0 Convert (1011)_2 to decimal. Write the place value under each digit. \begin{array}{cccc} 1 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 2^3 & 2^2 & 2^1 & 2^0 \\ 8 & 4 & 2 & 1 \end{array} Multiply each digit by its place value. \begin{aligned} 1 \cdot 8 &= 8 \\ 0 \cdot 4 &= 0 \\ 1 \cdot 2 &= 2 \\ 1 \cdot 1 &= 1 \end{aligned} Add the contributions: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11. (1011)_2 = 11 Convert (257)_8 to decimal. List the place values from the right: 1, 8, 64. Weight each digit. \begin{aligned} 2 \cdot 64 &= 128 \\ 5 \cdot 8 &= 40 \\ 7 \cdot 1 &= 7 \end{aligned} Add: 128 + 40 + 7 = 175. (257)_8 = 175 For which base b is (31)_b = 16? Expand the left side: (31)_b = 3 \cdot b + 1. Solve 3b + 1 = 16, which gives b = 5. Check the digits: 3 < 5 and 1 < 5, so (31)_5 is a valid numeral. b = 5 Why every number has one spelling Every whole number N \ge 0 has exactly one numeral in base b without leading zeros. The last digit is forced: every other term is a multiple of b, so d_0 is the remainder of N \div b. Remove it, divide by b, and the next digit is forced the same way. Repeat until nothing is left. Since no step had a choice, no two numerals can share a value. What is (110)_2 in decimal? 1 \cdot 4 + 1 \cdot 2 + 0 \cdot 1 = 6. Read binary left to right in your head: start at 0; for each bit, double the total and add the bit. For 1011: 0 \to 1 \to 2 \to 5 \to 11. It is the chain form from the derivation. "(19)_8" is not an octal numeral, because 9 is not an octal digit. In equations like (43)_x = (y3)_8 this quietly adds the conditions x > 4 and y < 8, and missing them gives wrong counts. Practice Positions to the right of the point continue the pattern: b^{-1}, b^{-2}, … So (0.1)_2 = \tfrac12. A digit is worth digit × b^{\text{position}}, counting positions from 0 on the right. Every digit must be smaller than the base. To read fast, use the chain: multiply by b, add the next digit.
